summary.seg: This edition of the Commedia is one of three printed in 1472. The name of the printer, Magistro Federico Veronensi, is recorded in the colophon as well as the date the book was produced ‘MCCCCLXXII quintodecimo [cal]alendas Augusti [i.e. 18 July 1472]. It was probably printed in Venice, but this information is not recorded inside the edition itself.

The poem is printed in a single column of roman type, with a typeface somewhat smaller than that of the edition printed in Foligno in 1472. Less attention seems to have been paid to the printing in comparison to the other copies printed in 1472, with no foliation, signatures, or catchwords. There is, moreover, a marked inconsistency in the way the cantos are titled. Some canti are introduced with short rubrics noting a major feature of the narrative, others are marked only by a blank space for the initial capital, and some are separated by two blank lines. Guide letters are occasionally present in the blank spaces at the start of the canti. The start of Paradiso is marked with a larger blank space for the initial capital but is not given a new page. The start of Purgatorio is marked with a smaller space for the initial capital but is placed at the top of a new page. No editor is named in the closing colophon.

The Rylands copy has a number of the original printed pages missing, which have been skilfully replaced by manuscript facsimiles, including the hand-decorated first page of the text [fol. a1]. Other manuscript interventions are present sporadically throughout the text.

note.p: Title from first three lines of incipit on leaf [a1] recto.
Title as cited by ISTC: La Commedia.
Attributed to Iesi by Proctor, but see V. Scholderer in Gb Jb 1932, pages 110-13 (reprinted in Fifty Essays pages 131-34).

On leaf [b8]r, the last terzina duplicated with variants (O uoi che haueti ..., Vui che hauete ... ); on leaf [b8]v, the last two terzine duplicate, also with variants (E tosco che per la cita ..., O tosco ...), the last two terzine on leaf [b9]v where they are in their proper place; three lines have dropped out between the last line on [b9]r (che ben parean ...offesi) and the first on [b9]v (Et egli a me ... eresiarche").

supportDesc.support:
Paper, folded in Fo (folio) and 4to (quarto).
Leaves [e2], [e3], [f1], [f2], [p5] and [p6] are folio, the rest quarto.

foliation.p: Pencil foliation, probably by George Appleyard, on the upper right corner of rectos.
Eighteenth-century[?] red ink foliation on the upper outer corner of rectos, many partially cropped.

condition.p: Imperfect: wanting leaves [a1],[a10],[b1], which are supplied in manuscript facsimile; leaves [b9],[b10], [e1], [e10], [n1], [n10] from another copy (see: Ragazzini, S. Liber Dantis. L'edizione principe jesina della Commedia. Mantova: Editoriale Padus, 1974); wanting final blank leaf [y10].

decoNote.p: [a1]r: illuminated initial in gold with white vine-stem decoration in blue, green and maroon.
Blank spaces for initials are marked with printed guide letters.

additions.p: Frequent manuscript nota marks in a sixteenth-century hand; occasional marginalia and maniculae; ink and red pencil underlining.
Seventeenth-century manuscript headline on [h3]v: Comedia 2.a di Dante dove si tratta del Purgatorio.

Nineteenth-century pencil note in an unknown hand on recto of rear fly-leaf: This Volume is printed in the same character as the Constitutiones Marchiae Anconitanae, printed by Federico Veronensis in the following year, in the colophon of which it is said to be printed in civitate Exii.

binding.p: Late eighteenth- or early nineteenth-century binding in dark green straight-grained goatskin over wooden boards.

The binding features a blind-tooled border of a palmette roll between fillets, with an inner panel of blind double fillets and curved lines at the corners. It is sewn on five supports, with five double raised bands. The board edges have a single gilt fillet, and the turn-ins are decorated with a gilt zig-zag and annulet roll. The endpapers are marbled.
The front cover features the nineteenth-century monogram of The John Rylands Library, JR within a roundel, stamped in gilt.
The spine is diveded in six compartments, heavily blind-tooled, with five gilt-tooled raised bands. The second and fifthe comartments are gilt-lettered: DANTE | A FEDERICO VERONENSI 1472

accMat.p: Ephemera: folded leaf of paper loosely inserted at front, with nineteenth-century manuscript annotation, which documents the missing leaves: Dante - Iesi - 1472. P copy can supply Leaf 19 ... 20 ... 41 ... 50 ... 121 ... 130 ... 6 leaves. Still wanting Leaf 1 ... 10 ... 11 ... which are in MS. in S copy, & are not in P copy. Leaf 175 ... reprinted on the reverse, word for word. 2 omission or dup: see another Dante.

provenance.p: ▪ George John Spencer, 2nd Earl Spencer (1758-1834), politician and book collectorSpencer, George John Spencer, Earl, 1758-1834
▪ John Poyntz Spencer, 5th Earl Spencer (1835-1910), politician and viceroy of IrelandSpencer, John Poyntz Spencer, Earl, 1835-1910

Originally part of the Spencer Library at Althorp, Northamptonshire, which was largely assembled by George Spencer, 2nd Earl Spencer, the collection later passed by descent to John Spencer, 5th Earl Spencer.
Oval leather label on the inner front cover: E BIBLIOTHECA SPENCERIANA.

Dibdin describes this copy (Bibliotheca Spenceriana, volume 4, number 813): The first leaf of the copy before us is supplied by a most skilfully executed ms. facsimile ... two leaves of ms. are unluckily introduced into the Vth Canto; and another similar leaf is in the Xth Canto.

acquisition.p: Acquired in 1892 by Enriqueta Rylands (1843-1908)Rylands, Enriqueta, 1843-1908 from John Poyntz Spencer, 5th Earl Spencer (1835-1910), for The John Rylands Library.

projectDesc.p: Created as part of the AHRC-funded research project: “Envisioning Dante, c. 1472-c. 1630: Seeing and Reading the Early Printed Page” (AH/W005220/1), on the Dante Alighieri early printed editions held at The John Rylands Research Institute and Library, led by Professor Guyda Armstrong (Principal Investigator, School of Arts, Languages and Cultures, The University of Manchester); Professor Simon Gilson (Co-Investigator, Faculty of Medieval and Modern Languages, University of Oxford); Dr Giles Bergel, Research Fellow (Visual Geometry Group, Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford); Dr Rebecca Bowen, Postdoctoral Research Associate (Faculty of Medieval and Modern Languages, University of Oxford), and Dr Gloria Moorman (School of Arts, Languages and Cultures, The University of Manchester).
